At this point we have three possible definitions of what it means for a
property <MATH_0001> of morphisms to be ``<ACCENT_0001>tale local on the source and
target'':
<STRUCT_0001>
<ITEMOPEN_0001>(ST)<ITEMCLOSE_0001> <MATH_0002> is <ACCENT_0002>tale local on the source and <MATH_0003> is
<ACCENT_0003>tale local on the target,
<ITEMOPEN_0002>(DM)<ITEMCLOSE_0002> (the definition in the paper <REF_0001> by
Deligne and Mumford) for every diagram
<MATH_0004>
with surjective <ACCENT_0004>tale vertical arrows we have
<MATH_0005>, and
<ITEMOPEN_0003>(SP)<ITEMCLOSE_0003> <MATH_0006> is <ACCENT_0005>tale local on the source-and-target.
<STRUCT_0002>
In this section we have seen that (SP) <MATH_0007> (DM) <MATH_0008> (ST).
The
Examples <REF_0002> and <REF_0003>
show that neither implication can be reversed. Finally,
Lemma <REF_0004>
shows that the difference disappears when looking at properties of
morphisms which are stable under postcomposing with open immersions, which
in practice will always be the case.
